title: White Smoke From Exhaust
summary: Common causes, likely diagnostic paths, OBD references, and repair-next steps for white smoke from the exhaust.
intro: White smoke from the exhaust can be simple condensation, but persistent white smoke with a sweet smell, rough running, or coolant loss usually means coolant is entering combustion or the exhaust stream. The first split is whether the smoke is brief and harmless on a cold morning or continues after the engine is fully warm.
common_sounds: White vapor that lingers after warm-up
Sweet-smelling exhaust in more serious cases
Rough idle or start-up misfire if one cylinder is affected
Coolant loss or overheating may appear with the smoke
quick_checks: Confirm whether the smoke clears fully after normal warm-up or stays present hot
Check coolant level and look for ongoing coolant loss before replacing bolt-on parts
Scan for misfire, coolant-temperature, and catalyst-efficiency codes
Inspect spark plugs if one cylinder is rough or likely coolant-fouled
Treat persistent sweet-smelling white smoke with overheating as a serious fault path
inspection_priority: Separate normal cold condensation from persistent hot smoke
Check coolant level, pressure, and contamination evidence
Inspect one-cylinder misfire clues before pricing simple bolt-on parts
confidence_cues: Head gasket possibility if smoke persists hot
common_causes: Normal condensation on a cold start
Coolant entering combustion or the exhaust stream
Start-up misfire from one coolant-fouled cylinder
Cooling-system problem contributing to repeated overheating
In some cases, overfueling or raw-fuel vapor can be mistaken for white smoke
diagnostic_paths: If the smoke disappears after warm-up and coolant level stays steady, condensation is more likely than a repair-grade fault.
If the smoke stays thick, sweet-smelling, and paired with coolant loss or overheating, an internal engine leak becomes more likely than a simple external bolt-on repair.
If the smoke is paired with a misfire on one cylinder, inspect plugs and cooling clues before assuming the fault is only ignition-related.

diagnostic_path_sections.title: Condensation vs Coolant Path
diagnostic_path_sections.summary: Use when smoke behavior changes after warm-up or coolant loss is uncertain.
checks: Confirm smoke clears fully after warm-up
Pressure test if coolant level drops
Inspect coolant and oil for cross-contamination

diagnostic_path_sections.title: Internal Leak and Misfire Path
diagnostic_path_sections.summary: Use when smoke persists hot, smells sweet, or one cylinder misfires after sitting.
checks: Inspect spark plugs for coolant cleaning or fouling
Check compression or leak-down if internal leakage is suspected
Treat overheating history as part of the estimate risk

recommended_repairs.title: Spark Plug Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Useful when one cylinder plug is fouled and a start-up misfire is part of the symptom path.

recommended_repairs.title: Cooling System Inspection
recommended_repairs.description: A reasonable next path when white smoke is paired with coolant loss and an external cooling failure is still part of the diagnosis.

recommended_repairs.title: Water Pump Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Relevant when overheating and poor coolant circulation are contributing to the cooling-side fault pattern.

recommended_repairs.title: Thermostat Blueprint
recommended_repairs.description: Worth pricing when temperature-control problems overlap with the exhaust-smoke complaint, but only after the more serious internal leak path is considered.

recommended_repairs.title: Head Gasket Possibility
recommended_repairs.description: Use careful diagnosis when persistent sweet white smoke, coolant loss, and misfire evidence point internal.

recommended_repairs.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Useful only when the temperature signal itself is misleading the cooling diagnosis rather than causing the smoke directly.
